title: Parliamentary Panel Presses IndiGo and Air India as Airlines Blame Fuel and Closed Skies
excerpt: The Committee on Public Undertakings, chaired by Baijayant Panda, questioned both carriers on November 2. IndiGo pointed to a Rs 1,879.1 crore quarterly loss and Air India to longer, costlier routings around Pakistan's closed airspace.
body:
• A parliamentary panel questioned IndiGo and Air India officials on Monday, November 2, over rising airfares; the airlines blamed surging jet fuel (ATF) prices and the closure of Pakistan's airspace, according to a source cited by PTI.
  • IndiGo recorded a loss of Rs 1,879.1 crore in the September quarter, which it attributed to high fuel costs and rupee depreciation; Air India's losses nearly doubled in 2025-26.
  • Pakistan's airspace closure, in place since early last year, forces Air India's Europe and North America flights onto longer routes with higher fuel burn and crew costs; the annualised impact on Air India alone was earlier estimated at around Rs 5,000 crore.
  • For travellers: no fare relief was announced at the meeting, and IndiGo has already raised its fuel charge on Gulf flights to Rs 5,500 per sector from October 6 — expect India fares to stay elevated while fuel and airspace conditions hold.

Air travel in India is likely to stay expensive, and Parliament has now asked the two biggest carriers why. A parliamentary panel on Monday raised concerns over rising airfares during a meeting with senior officials of IndiGo and Air India, who told members that surging jet fuel costs and the closure of Pakistan's airspace were pushing their operating costs higher, according to a source cited by PTI's report of the meeting.

The meeting

The issues were discussed at a meeting of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Public Undertakings, chaired by BJP member Baijayant Panda, on Monday, November 2. The panel met the airlines' officials in the second half of the day, after a meeting with the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS) and the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) earlier in the day. Some panel members flagged concerns about high airfares; in response, officials of both airlines pointed to rising aviation turbine fuel prices, the source said.

The airlines' numbers

IndiGo, the country's largest airline, recorded a loss of Rs 1,879.1 crore in the September quarter, which it attributed to high fuel costs and rupee depreciation. Its reported fuel cost per available seat kilometre rose 68.9 per cent even as yields — average revenue per passenger — rose 34.3 per cent, according to reporting of its quarterly figures. Air India, which has significant international operations, also saw its losses nearly double in 2025-26. IndiGo has already passed part of the pressure to passengers on some routes, raising its fuel charge on GCC flights to Rs 5,500 per sector from October 6.

The Pakistan airspace factor

Pakistan's airspace has been closed to Indian aircraft since early last year. For Air India, whose long-haul network leans west, that means Europe and North America services fly longer routes, burning more fuel and using more crew hours, while foreign competitors that can still use Pakistani airspace avoid those diversions. The closure's annualised financial impact on Air India alone was earlier estimated at around Rs 5,000 crore. This week the airline went further: it has proposed a per-litre levy on aviation fuel uplifted in India by Indian and foreign carriers alike, with collections used to give Indian carriers fuel discounts tied to the airspace burden, The Hindu BusinessLine reported on November 5. The proposal is not an approved policy — the levy rate, the allocation method and the government's response are all still open, and neither Air India nor the Civil Aviation Ministry commented to BusinessLine.

What it means for your ticket

Nothing in the week's developments points to cheaper fares soon. The panel meeting produced scrutiny, not a cap; the airlines' stated cost drivers — ATF prices and a closed airspace — are outside their control; and the one concrete relief proposal, Air India's fuel levy, is a request to government that has not been accepted. Diaspora travellers booking India trips for the winter season should treat current fare levels as the planning baseline, and watch two things: any government decision on the levy, and IndiGo's and Air India's next round of fuel-charge changes, which have been the first place cost pressure reaches the ticket price.
